los.text: Identify and side a clavicle, identify its main anatomical landmarks on the bone and on suitable radiographs, and name its articulations and muscular and ligamentous attachments
los.html:
Siding
  • Lateral end flat (acromial)
  • Medial end rounded (sternal)
  • Medial two-thirds convex forwards
  • Groove for subclavius and the conoid tubercle on the underside.
ArticulationsSternoclavicular (manubrium and 1st costal cartilage), acromioclavicular (acromion).
AttachmentWhere on the clavicle
Sternocleidomastoid (clavicular head)Upper surface, medial third
Pectoralis majorFront, medial half
DeltoidFront, lateral third
TrapeziusBack, lateral third
SubclaviusGroove underneath
Costoclavicular ligamentUnderside, medial end
Coracoclavicular ligamentConoid tubercle and trapezoid line, underside lateral end
  • Facts: first bone to ossify (in membrane, week 5–6)
    • medial epiphysis fuses last (~25 years)
    • S-shaped on X-ray
    • most fractures in the middle third.

los.text: Identify and side a scapula, identify its main anatomical landmarks, and name its articulations and muscular and ligamentous attachments
los.html:
Landmarks
  • Spine (separates supraspinous and infraspinous fossae)
  • Acromion
  • Coracoid process
  • Glenoid cavity
  • Supraglenoid and infraglenoid tubercles
  • Subscapular fossa
  • Suprascapular notch
  • Medial/lateral/superior borders
  • Superior and inferior angles (inferior angle ≈ T7).
ArticulationsGlenohumeral, acromioclavicular; scapulothoracic (a functional joint: scapula gliding on the ribs).
RegionMuscles
FossaeSupraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis
Lateral borderTeres minor (upper), teres major (lower, near inferior angle)
Medial borderSerratus anterior (front), rhomboids and levator scapulae (back)
Spine and acromionTrapezius, deltoid
CoracoidPectoralis minor, short head of biceps, coracobrachialis
TuberclesSupraglenoid: long head of biceps; infraglenoid: long head of triceps
  • Ligaments: coracoacromial (roof over the shoulder), coracoclavicular, glenohumeral, coracohumeral, transverse scapular (over the notch).

los.text: Explain that the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints are atypical synovial joints, with fibrocartilage lining the articular surfaces
los.html:
Both joints are "atypical" synovial jointsThe articular surfaces are covered by fibrocartilage, not hyaline, because the clavicle forms by intramembranous ossification.
Sternoclavicular
  • Saddle-type with an articular disc dividing it into two cavities
  • The only bony joint between upper limb and axial skeleton
  • Very stable.
AcromioclavicularPlane joint (sometimes an incomplete disc); stability comes mainly from the coracoclavicular ligament.

los.text: Identify the sternoclavicular (anterior and posterior), costoclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments, and be aware that these strong ligaments mean that the clavicle rarely dislocates, and instead is the most commonly fractured bone
los.html:
Ligaments
  • Anterior and posterior sternoclavicular
  • Interclavicular
  • Costoclavicular (clavicle to 1st rib; the strongest)
  • Coracoclavicular (conoid + trapezoid; hangs the scapula and arm from the clavicle).
SoThe clavicle rarely dislocates and is instead the most commonly fractured bone (fall on the shoulder or outstretched hand).
Fracture deformity
  • Medial fragment pulled up by sternocleidomastoid
  • Lateral fragment pulled down by the weight of the arm and in by pectoralis major: drooping shoulder.
RisksSubclavian vessels and brachial plexus underneath (rare).
ACJ separationAC ± coracoclavicular ligament tear → step deformity.

los.text: Locate the muscles: serratus anterior, pectoralis minor, pectoralis major, subclavius, latissimus dorsi, trapezius, levator scapulae, rhomboid minor, rhomboid major, deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, teres major, and subscapularis
los.html:
GroupMuscles and where they lie
Anterior chest
  • Pectoralis major (anterior axillary fold)
  • Pectoralis minor (under it, ribs 3–5 to coracoid)
  • Subclavius (under clavicle)
  • Serratus anterior (side of chest wall, ribs 1–8)
Superficial backTrapezius (upper back and neck), latissimus dorsi (lower back to the posterior axillary fold)
Deep backLevator scapulae (side of neck to superior angle), rhomboid minor and major (spine to medial border, under trapezius)
ScapulohumeralDeltoid (cap of shoulder), supraspinatus (above spine), infraspinatus (below spine), teres minor and major (lateral border), subscapularis (front of scapula)
  • Axillary folds: anterior = pectoralis major; posterior = latissimus dorsi + teres major.

los.text: Describe the actions of the muscles acting on the shoulder girdle (scapula and clavicle) summarising their main attachments and somatic nervous innervation
los.html:
MuscleAttachmentsNerveAction on the girdle
TrapeziusOcciput, ligamentum nuchae, C7–T12 spines → lateral clavicle, acromion, scapular spineAccessory (XI)Upper: elevate + upward rotation; middle: retract; lower: depress + upward rotation
Levator scapulaeC1–4 transverse processes → superior angleDorsal scapular (C5) + C3–4Elevate, downward rotation
Rhomboids (minor, major)Spines C7–T5 → medial borderDorsal scapular (C5)Retract, downward rotation
Serratus anteriorRibs 1–8 → medial border (front)Long thoracic (C5–7)Protract, upward rotation (arm above 90°)
Pectoralis minorRibs 3–5 → coracoidMedial pectoral (C8–T1)Depress, protract
Subclavius1st rib → clavicleNerve to subclavius (C5–6)Anchors the clavicle
Upward rotation(to raise the arm overhead)Trapezius + serratus anterior. Downward rotation: levator scapulae, rhomboids, pectoralis minor.
InjuriesLong thoracic nerve → winged scapula; accessory nerve → can't shrug, drooping shoulder.

los.text: Identify and side a humerus, identify its main anatomical landmarks and name its articulations and muscular and ligamentous attachments
los.html:
ProximalHead (faces medially, up, back), anatomical neck, greater tubercle (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor), lesser tubercle (subscapularis), intertubercular groove (long head of biceps; "lady between two majors": pectoralis major on the lateral lip, latissimus in the floor, teres major on the medial lip), surgical neck.
ShaftDeltoid tuberosity (lateral, midshaft); radial (spiral) groove behind.
Distal
  • Medial epicondyle (common flexor origin; ulnar nerve behind it)
  • Lateral epicondyle (common extensor origin)
  • Trochlea (ulna)
  • Capitulum (radial head)
  • Olecranon fossa behind
  • Coronoid and radial fossae in front.
SidingHead points medially; olecranon fossa is posterior; medial epicondyle is the bigger one.
Fracture siteStructure at risk
Surgical neckAxillary nerve, posterior circumflex humeral artery
MidshaftRadial nerve, profunda brachii
SupracondylarMedian nerve, brachial artery
Medial epicondyleUlnar nerve

los.text: Describe the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint as a large, synovial, ball-and-socket joint, identify the rotator cuff muscles, their actions, and recall the movements of this joint
los.html:
Type
  • Synovial ball-and-socket
  • The glenoid covers only about a third of the head, deepened by the fibrocartilage glenoid labrum: mobility at the cost of stability.
CapsuleLax, weakest inferiorly; glenohumeral ligaments thicken it in front; coracohumeral ligament above; coracoacromial arch roofs the joint.
Long head of bicepsRuns inside the joint, wrapped in synovium.
Rotator cuff (SITS)ActionNerve
SupraspinatusStarts abduction (0–15°)Suprascapular
InfraspinatusLateral rotationSuprascapular
Teres minorLateral rotationAxillary
SubscapularisMedial rotationUpper and lower subscapular
MovementMain muscles
FlexionPectoralis major (clavicular), anterior deltoid, coracobrachialis, biceps
ExtensionPosterior deltoid, latissimus dorsi, teres major
AbductionSupraspinatus 0–15°, deltoid 15–90°, trapezius + serratus anterior above 90°
AdductionPectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major
Medial rotationSubscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus, teres major
Lateral rotationInfraspinatus, teres minor, posterior deltoid
  • Subacromial bursa: between cuff and acromion: inflamed in impingement.

los.text: Explain why the shoulder is the most commonly dislocated joint, recall that it dislocates inferiorly, and predict the functional and possible pathological consequences of this type of injury
los.html:
Why it dislocates most
  • Shallow glenoid, lax capsule, mobility over stability
  • The inferior capsule has no rotator cuff support, so the head escapes downwards first.
Where it ends upUsually anterior (subcoracoid, ~95%) after a fall on an abducted, externally rotated arm; posterior after seizures or electric shock.
Consequences
  • Axillary nerve injury (wraps round the surgical neck) → weak deltoid and teres minor, numb "regimental badge" patch
  • Bankart lesion (anterior labral tear)
  • Hill–Sachs lesion (dent in the posterolateral head)
  • Rotator cuff tear in older patients
  • Recurrent instability.
Check and document axillary nerve sensation before and after reduction.

los.text: Identify the boundaries and contents of the axilla
los.html:
PartFormed by
Apex (cervico-axillary canal)Clavicle, 1st rib, upper border of scapula
BaseSkin and fascia of the armpit
Anterior wallPectoralis major and minor, subclavius, clavipectoral fascia
Posterior wallSubscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi
Medial wallSerratus anterior over ribs 1–4
Lateral wallIntertubercular groove; coracobrachialis and biceps
Contents
  • Axillary artery (3 parts by pectoralis minor) and vein (medial)
  • Brachial plexus cords and branches
  • Axillary lymph nodes (pectoral, subscapular, humeral, central, apical)
  • Fat
  • Long thoracic nerve on the medial wall.
Clinical~75% of breast lymph drains here; axillary clearance risks the long thoracic and thoracodorsal nerves.

los.text: Label a diagram of the brachial plexus, and identify the parts of the plexus on a model or a prosection
los.html:
PartDetail
RootsVentral rami C5–T1, between anterior and middle scalenes
TrunksUpper (C5–6), middle (C7), lower (C8–T1): posterior triangle of neck
DivisionsAnterior and posterior of each trunk: behind the clavicle
CordsLateral (anterior divisions of upper + middle), medial (anterior division of lower), posterior (all posterior divisions): named by position around the axillary artery behind pectoralis minor
Terminal branchesMusculocutaneous (lateral cord), median (lateral + medial cords), ulnar (medial cord), axillary and radial (posterior cord)
LevelOther branches
RootsDorsal scapular (C5), long thoracic (C5–7)
Upper trunkSuprascapular (C5–6), nerve to subclavius
Lateral cordLateral pectoral
Medial cordMedial pectoral, medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm
Posterior cordUpper and lower subscapular, thoracodorsal (latissimus)
  • Order: "Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer": roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches.

los.text: Explain the loss of function resulting from injuries to the different parts of the brachial plexus
los.html:
InjuryCauseResult
Erb's palsy (upper trunk, C5–6)Head and shoulder forced apart: shoulder dystocia, motorbike fall"Waiter's tip": arm adducted and medially rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated; numb lateral arm
Klumpke's palsy (lower trunk, C8–T1)Arm pulled up: grabbing a branch, breech deliveryClaw hand (intrinsic muscles lost), numb medial forearm and hand; ± Horner's (T1 sympathetic)
Long thoracic nerveAxillary surgery, carrying heavy loadsWinged scapula
Root avulsionSevere tractionWorse prognosis; may include Horner's

los.text: Recall the origins and functions of the axillary, radial, ulnar, musculocutaneous and median nerves in the arm, forearm, wrist and hand
los.html:
Nerve (roots, cord)CourseFunction
Axillary (C5–6, posterior)Quadrangular space with posterior circumflex humeral artery, round the surgical neckDeltoid, teres minor; skin over lower deltoid
Radial (C5–T1, posterior)Spiral groove with profunda brachii → in front of lateral epicondyle → superficial (sensory) and deep/posterior interosseous (motor) branchesExtensors of elbow, wrist, fingers and thumb; supinator, brachioradialis
Musculocutaneous (C5–7, lateral)Pierces coracobrachialis → between biceps and brachialis → lateral cutaneous nerve of forearmElbow flexion, supination (biceps)
Median (C5–T1, lateral + medial)
  • With brachial artery (no branches in the arm)
  • → cubital fossa
  • → between pronator teres heads
  • → between FDS and FDP
  • → carpal tunnel
Most forearm flexors and pronators; LOAF in the hand
Ulnar (C8–T1, medial)Behind the medial epicondyle → between FCU heads → with ulnar artery → Guyon's canalFCU, medial FDP, most small hand muscles

los.text: Name the main muscles and muscle groups that the axillary, radial, ulnar, musculocutaneous and median nerves supply and their sensory distribution
los.html:
NerveMusclesSkin
MusculocutaneousAnterior arm: coracobrachialis, biceps, brachialisLateral forearm
AxillaryDeltoid, teres minor"Regimental badge" over lower deltoid
RadialPosterior arm (triceps, anconeus); posterior forearm (extensors, supinator, brachioradialis)Back of arm and forearm; lateral back of hand (1st dorsal web space)
Median
  • Anterior forearm except FCU and medial FDP
  • Anterior interosseous (FPL, lateral FDP, pronator quadratus)
  • LOAF: lateral 2 lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis
Palmar lateral 3½ digits and their nail beds
UlnarFCU, medial FDP; hypothenar, all interossei, medial 2 lumbricals, adductor pollicisMedial 1½ digits, front and back
  • Shortcut: anterior arm = musculocutaneous
    • anterior forearm = median (+ ulnar 1½ muscles)
    • everything posterior = radial
    • hand = ulnar except LOAF.

los.text: Predict the consequences of common injuries to the axillary, radial, ulnar, musculocutaneous and median nerves and describe how to test their functional integrity
los.html:
NerveTypical injurySignQuick test
AxillaryShoulder dislocation, surgical neck fractureWeak abduction, flat deltoidSensation over regimental badge
RadialMidshaft fracture, "Saturday night" palsy (spiral groove); crutch palsy (axilla, triceps too)Wrist dropExtend wrist and fingers against resistance; sensation on dorsal 1st web space
MusculocutaneousPenetrating injury (rare)Weak elbow flexion and supination, no biceps reflexLateral forearm sensation
MedianCarpal tunnel or wrist cut (distal); supracondylar fracture (proximal)Thenar wasting, lost opposition ("ape hand"); proximal lesion: hand of benediction on making a fistAbduct thumb against resistance; index pulp sensation; OK sign (anterior interosseous)
UlnarMedial epicondyle/elbow (cubital tunnel), wrist cutClaw of ring and little fingers (worse with a wrist lesion: the "ulnar paradox"); hypothenar and interossei wastingFroment's sign; spread fingers against resistance; little finger sensation
